hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 adheres more tightly to some recycling receptors than APOE3, impeding recycling.

rows.Finding description: Confocal microscopy showed loss of LRP1 from astrocyte processes and greater perinuclear LRP1 accumulation in APOE4 than APOE3 mouse astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: Confocal microscopy revealed a striking loss of LRP1 from astrocyte processes and increased perinuclear accumulation in ApoE4 cells, relative to ApoE3 ( Fig. 2 F ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (greater intracellular LRP1 accumulation and less LRP1 in processes)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. Fixed-cell LRP1 immunofluorescence assessed by confocal microscopy, including orthogonal sections. Static receptor distribution, not a direct recycling-rate or apoE-binding assay; not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Restoring NHE6 expression in APOE4 mouse astrocytes increased surface-biotinylated LRP1 approximately 5.7-fold relative to empty vector in three biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: Similar results were obtained in surface biotinylation experiments that showed robust, ∼5.7-fold higher surface LRP1 levels in ApoE4 cells with restored NHE6 expression, compared with transfection with empty vector ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 C ).
rows.Finding summary: (NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain unstated. Lentiviral NHE6-GFP expression versus empty vector; cell-surface biotinylation and LRP1 immunoblotting in three biological replicates. Expression duration unstated. Not human brain cells.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S7C, surface LRP1 comparison

rows.Finding description: Surface biotinylation showed approximately 50% lower plasma-membrane LRP1 in APOE4 than APOE3 mouse astrocytes in three biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: First, surface biotinylation revealed that plasma membrane expression of LRP1 receptor in ApoE4 astrocytes was lower by ∼50% ( Fig. 2 B ).
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with isogenic human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. Surface biotinylation and immunoblotting, normalized using plasma-membrane Na+/K+-ATPase, in three biological replicates. Measures receptor surface abundance, not apoE–LRP1 binding strength; not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Live-cell surface antibody labeling found approximately 55% fewer LRP1-positive APOE4 than APOE3 mouse astrocytes in three biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: Second, an antibody directed against an external epitope of LRP1 to quantify surface expression in live cells by flow cytometry analysis showed a reduction of LRP1-positive cells by ∼55% in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig. 2 C ) and by ∼51% in patient-derived ApoE4/4 fibroblasts ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 D ).
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. Live, nonpermeabilized cells labeled on ice with external-epitope anti-LRP1 antibody and analyzed by flow cytometry; Fig 2C specifies 10,000 cells in biological triplicates. Not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Surface immunofluorescence showed approximately 49% lower LRP1 labeling in APOE4 than APOE3 mouse astrocytes.
rows.Finding quote: Third, this was confirmed by confocal microscopy showing ∼49% lower LRP1 surface labeling by antibody in ApoE4 ( Fig. 2 D ).
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. Live-cell external-epitope anti-LRP1 labeling on ice for one hour, followed by fixation, secondary antibody labeling and confocal microscopy; n=75 per condition. Not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Expressing wild-type NHE6 in APOE4 mouse astrocytes increased surface LRP1 staining approximately 2.5-fold relative to vector-transfected APOE4 cells.
rows.Finding quote: Compared with the weak surface LRP1 staining in vector-transfected ApoE4 astrocytes, we observed prominent, ∼2.5-fold higher LRP1 staining in ApoE4 cells expressing ectopic NHE6 ( Fig. 4 F ).
rows.Finding summary: (NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. Lentiviral expression of wild-type NHE6-GFP versus empty vector; surface immunofluorescence in nonpermeabilized cells, n=40 per condition. Treatment duration not stated; not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: NHE6 expression in APOE4 mouse astrocytes reduced perinuclear LRP1 accumulation and partially restored LRP1 staining on astrocyte processes toward the APOE3 pattern.
rows.Finding quote: Consistent with these findings, confocal microscopy revealed a reduction in perinuclear accumulation of LRP1 and partial restoration of staining on astrocyte processes in ApoE4 cells with NHE6 expression ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 E ).
rows.Finding summary: (NHE6 expression in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (less perinuclear LRP1 and restored process localization)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background, with APOE3 astrocytes as a reference; age and strain unstated. NHE6-GFP expression and fixed-cell LRP1 confocal immunofluorescence. Treatment duration and sample size unstated. Not human brain cells; static localization rather than recycling kinetics.

rows.Finding description: TSA treatment of APOE4 mouse astrocytes increased surface LRP1 approximately twofold compared with vehicle in three biological replicates.
rows.Finding quote: Importantly, we observed prominent, approximately twofold higher surface LRP1 expression in ApoE4 cells with TSA treatment ( Fig. 5 E and SI Appendix , Fig. S8 G ).
rows.Finding summary: (TSA treatment in APOE4 astrocytes) -> (higher surface LRP1)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. TSA, 5 μM for 12 hours, versus DMSO; surface LRP1 labeling at 4°C and flow cytometry in biological triplicates. Not human brain cells; HDAC inhibition is a pleiotropic intervention.

rows.Finding description: During the LRP1 internalization assay, APOE4 mouse astrocytes showed lower surface LRP1 staining than APOE3 astrocytes; no between-genotype effect magnitude or P value was reported for this panel.
rows.Finding quote: Note lower LRP1 staining in ApoE4 astrocytes, relative to ApoE3, due to reduced surface expression.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (lower surface LRP1 during internalization assay)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain unstated. Cells labeled with external-epitope anti-LRP1 on ice, incubated at 4°C or 37°C for 10 minutes, then remaining surface antibody detected on ice by secondary labeling and flow cytometry; biological triplicates. Not human brain cells.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Fig S4D, between-genotype surface-staining comparison

rows.Finding description: An on-ice ligand-binding assay found 66% less surface-bound Aβ on APOE4 than APOE3 mouse astrocytes; the ligand was Aβ, so this does not measure apoE–receptor adhesion.
rows.Finding quote: In a fourth approach, surface-bound ligand (fluorescent Aβ) measured by confocal microscopy was 66% lower in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig. 2 E ).
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain not stated. After 30-minute serum starvation, 100 nM fluorescent Aβ in 1% BSA was applied on ice for 10 minutes, followed by washing, fixation and confocal quantification; n=75 per condition. Not human brain cells.

rows.Finding description: Surface antibody labeling found approximately 51% lower LRP1 positivity in APOE4/4 AD-patient fibroblasts than in age-matched APOE3/3 control fibroblasts.
rows.Finding quote: Second, an antibody directed against an external epitope of LRP1 to quantify surface expression in live cells by flow cytometry analysis showed a reduction of LRP1-positive cells by ∼55% in ApoE4 astrocytes ( Fig. 2 C ) and by ∼51% in patient-derived ApoE4/4 fibroblasts ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 D ).
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3/3 control fibroblasts -> APOE4/4 AD fibroblasts) -> (lower surface LRP1 positivity)
rows.Experimental system: Human primary fibroblast lines APOE3/3 AG04387 and AD-patient-derived APOE4/4 AG10788; age matched, exact ages unstated. External-epitope anti-LRP1 labeling of live, nonpermeabilized cells on ice, followed by flow cytometry in biological triplicates. Nonisogenic, nonbrain cells; APOE4 donor has AD.

rows.Finding description: APOE3 and APOE4 mouse astrocytes showed no significant difference in normalized LRP1 internalization over 10 minutes; this null concerns endocytosis rather than return recycling.
rows.Finding quote: The rate of LRP1 endocytosis (at 37 °C for 10 min) in ApoE3 and ApoE4 astrocytes was similar ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 ), suggesting that LRP1 delivery by exocytosis or recycling may contribute to the differences in surface expression.
rows.Finding summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in normalized LRP1 internalization)
rows.Experimental system: Cultured mouse astrocytes with human APOE3 or APOE4 knock-in on an ApoE-knockout background; age and strain unstated. External-epitope anti-LRP1 labeling on ice, 10-minute incubation at 37°C versus 4°C, and flow-cytometric measurement of remaining surface antibody; normalized internalization compared in biological triplicates. Not human brain cells.

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: At 300–310 K, 11.12% of simulated ApoE4 conformations versus 0.05% of ApoE3 conformations met the authors' intermediate-similarity criterion.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE Isoform Population of Intermediate from 300 to 310 K E2 70.66 % E3 0.05 % E4 11.12 %
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher simulated intermediate-like conformational population at 300–310 K)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomers in implicit-solvent REX/DMD; conformations at 300–310 K classified against each isoform's own T3 intermediate centroid using N-terminal helical RMSD less than 15 Å; no human brain cells, endo-lysosomes, or intermolecular aggregation.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 4, E3 and E4 rows

rows.Finding description: The summary table reports intermediate-like populations of 11.1% for ApoE4 versus 0.1% for ApoE3 at 300–310 K, using rounded values from Supplementary Table 4.
rows.Finding quote: Population of Intermediate from 300 to 310 K E2 70.66 % E3 0.05 % E4 11.12 %
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (higher simulated intermediate-like population at 300–310 K)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomer REX/DMD; intermediate-like conformations defined by N-terminal helical RMSD less than 15 Å from each isoform's own intermediate centroid; rounded summary of Supplementary Table 4, not independent evidence.
rows.Data location: Supplementary Table 7, Population of intermediate state at 300 to 310 K row

rows.Finding description: Intermediate-state clustering showed two separating helix pairs in ApoE3 but separation of helix–1 alone in ApoE4, which the authors identified as a unique misfolded intermediate.
rows.Finding quote: Specifically, we observe a decrease in the hydrophobic contacts of ApoE2’s N-terminal domain helices (Fig 3B) and ApoE3’s N-terminal domain separating into two helix pairs (Fig 3C). More importantly, we identify a unique intermediate state for ApoE4 (Discussion section), in which only helix–1 separates from the N-terminal domain helix bundle (Fig 3D).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (isoform-specific simulated misfolded intermediate with separated helix–1)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomers in implicit-solvent REX/DMD; centroid structures of the most populated N-terminal RMSD clusters from PMF basins; ApoE3 at 338 K and ApoE4 at 328 K; no apoE oligomers or cellular compartments modeled.

rows.Finding description: At their respective intermediate temperatures, simulated ApoE4 occupied a distinct, more compact conformational landscape than ApoE3, consistent with an isoform-specific misfolded monomer.
rows.Finding quote: ApoE3 is characterized by both the native and alternate N-terminal domain conformations, while ApoE2 visits only the latter. ApoE4 exhibits a unique, more compact intermediate conformational state as denoted by the smaller range of RMSD and Rg values compared to the two other variants.
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (distinct, more compact simulated intermediate conformational landscape)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomer models in implicit-solvent REX/DMD; ApoE3 at 338 K versus ApoE4 at 328 K; potential-of-mean-force landscapes using N-terminal helical Cα RMSD and radius of gyration, excluding the flexible C-terminal domain from reaction coordinates; no cellular or endo-lysosomal system.

rows.Finding description: At intermediate temperatures, simulated ApoE3 lacked inter-domain contacts while ApoE4 retained contacts linking residues 26–44, 196–215, and 235–243.
rows.Finding quote: Interestingly, for ApoE4 at temperature T3, we observe a unique series of contacts between residues 26 to 44 in the N-terminal helix–1, residues 196 to 215 in the hinge region, and residues 235 to 243 in the C-terminal domain (Fig 4I outlined in red).
rows.Finding summary: (ApoE3 -> ApoE4) -> (retained isoform-specific inter-domain contacts in the simulated misfolded intermediate)
rows.Experimental system: Human full-length apoE monomers, implicit-solvent REX/DMD; ApoE3 at 338 K versus ApoE4 at 328 K; pairwise distance analysis of the intermediate ensembles; reported ApoE4 contacts involve N-terminal helix–1, hinge/C-terminal boundary, and C-terminal residues; no measured oligomers or endo-lysosomal localization.
rows.Data location: Fig 4H–I; Results, Inter-domain interactions of ApoE isoforms

hypothesis: In some types of non-Alzheimer's, non-aged human brain cells, APOE4 undergoes increased aggregation in the endo-lysosome compared with APOE3.

rows.Finding description: Across three LysoIP replicates, human-APOE4-expressing murine Neuro-2a cells showed greater lysosomal APOE abundance than human-APOE3-expressing cells, providing an accumulation surrogate without measuring apoE aggregation.
rows.Finding quote: Through this approach, we found that HsAPOE4-expressing lysosomes accumulated APOE itself, AD-associated secretase proteins (PSEN2, CD63, TSPAN3), trafficking receptors (AP1S1, AP1G1, BET1L, LAMTOR1, LAMTOR2, TMED5), and lipid/glycan-regulators (ACSL4, ACBD3, GALNT2, MAN2B1, NEU1, PIP4P1, SACM1L, PIP4P1/TMEM55B, UXS1) (Figure 3B,C, Figure S3C).
rows.Experimental system: Male murine Neuro-2a neuroblastoma cells carrying full-length human APOE3 or APOE4 genomic transgenes; endogenous mouse Apoe retained; passages 5–10; basal untreated condition; TMEM192-3xHA LysoIP followed by quantitative DIA mass spectrometry with lysosomal-tag normalization.
